Item number 4.01 is the presentation on collective bargaining from the school board came to the legislative committee a motion to draft a collective bargaining resolution to later present to the full school board.

And as part of doing that, the Legislative and Policy Committee has invited the Loudoun Education Association to present their suggested collective bargaining agreement to us. So I'm going to go ahead and turn it over to Ms. Sandy Sullivan to start your portion of the presentation.

Excellent. Thank you very much, Chair Reeser. Good afternoon. We appreciate the time set aside for LEA to present information about our collective bargaining resolution.

Joining me in presenting is Corey Brunet, EL teacher from Broad Run, and Mariah Allen. She's Virginia Education Association staff attorney. LEA presented the school board with substantial evidence of employee support for collective bargaining. As we went about gathering union authorization cards from our colleagues, we had conversations about the importance of having a meaningful seat at the table so that the individuals who work closest with the students have the resources they need to provide every child a quality education. Winning the right to collective bargaining around salaries, benefits, and working conditions is that meaningful seat at

the table. From here, the path to collective bargaining is a school board resolution. It is the resolution that establishes the framework and the process for employees to elect a bargaining representative and for the bargaining representative and LCPS to come together and negotiate in good faith. Next slide, please. So our presentation will cover our goals for collective bargaining resolution, specific items that are in our resolution, what would occur after a resolution is passed, how LEA plans to approach collective bargaining, and then we'll answer questions that

you have. So when the General Assembly allowed for local governing bodies to adopt collective bargaining if they so choose, they really didn't give a lot of guidance or set many parameters. It's at the school board's discretion. We carefully drafted our proposed resolution with the five goals on this slide in mind. Implementing collective burden should not result in steep costs and should not require hiring additional staff or experts. Our proposed resolution envisions administrators sitting down with their employees to come to mutual agreement over working conditions and ways to improve schools and where disputes arise or there are allegations

that the collective bargaining resolution is not being followed our proposed collective bargaining resolution calls for school board involvement in the dispute resolution process just as the school board is now involved in hearing and deciding employee grievances and enforcing its own policies the structure should feel familiar and comfortable to school board members next slide so first I'll provide an overview of the entire resolution, and then we'll go through each major section independently. Policy statements. Those are the whereas clauses with declarations regarding commitment to collective bargaining and what it

has the potential to achieve. There are definitions, for example, what is meant by benefits and collective bargaining, and also which employees may be included in collective bargaining. Rights of employees. Much of this language is modeled on federal labor law, the National Labor Relations Act. Employee rights include being allowed to speak with one another about the union and about working conditions, joining and supporting a union, or deciding not to do any of those things. In terms of employer or management rights, collective bargaining will not infringe upon certain school board decisions that are inherently and exclusively

managerial, like hiring, drafting job descriptions, and establishing budget. Duties and rights of an exclusive representative. The exclusive representative is the union that has been elected by employees to represent them in bargaining. The resolution gives this union the right to bargain with LCPS as well as other rights to ensure that it can meaningfully represent employees, like the right to employee contact information and to meet with employees in their work site. Procedures for conducting elections. That entails what's required to

schedule an election and who may call for an election. Procedures for how exactly bargaining will work and what will happen if two sides can't come to an agreement, an impasse, and a provision on prohibited conduct or unfair labor practices. This includes what happens if a union or the employer violate employee rights by coercing them into supporting or not supporting the union or by retaliating against them for supporting or not supporting the union. This also includes what happens if administrators or the union is bargaining in bad faith. And also the collective bargaining resolution spells out what conduct is prohibited and how

allegations are raised heard and resolved next slide please can you hear me from here okay thank you Sandy it's nice to meet you all I'm Mariah Allen I am a staff attorney at the VA I'm one of the architects of the resolution that LEA has proposed and I'm supporting our locals around Virginia as they organize and push for collective bargaining.

It's really a pleasure to share this space with you, and I appreciate the time. I want to just also say hi to Mr. Falcone over there. It's nice to see you in person. We've had the opportunity to Zoom, but I appreciate being able to be in this space with you all.

I worked at the National Labor Relations Board, which, as Sandy mentioned, the National Labor Relations Act is the federal labor policy. So that's where my experience comes from as a labor lawyer, and I was in their New York City regional office. So that's a bit of my background and kind of what's informing part of this effort.

When we say we modeled provisions on federal labor policy, that's very accurate. So I want to just go with you a little bit through the sections of the resolution, And I'll try to be quick and brief because I think, you know, the LEA folks are the people who you should really be hearing from.

But, you know, this would be a new policy, and I just want to be available to answer questions and make sure we can understand some of the decisions we made about the language that we included and the goals that we're trying to achieve. So the first kind of meaty section of the resolution is the definitions.

And it's there that we set forth two proposed bargaining units. I know that as LEA initially presented you with certification that it had majority support for collective bargaining. It focused on one cohort, and that was classroom teachers.

But the state statute allows you, the school board, to deem any other Loudoun County Public Schools employees appropriate for collective bargaining rights. And it's our position that that should be broad, and we have created a definition of employee that is broad, but a separate definition for administrative employees, and not including them in the two bargaining units that we have set forth.

So we have proposed a unit of certified employees and then a unit of school support staff or non-certified employees in two separate bargaining cohorts so that the contracts you would be negotiating would be a separate one for school support staff and a separate one for certified or licensed staff.
with the understanding that there has to be some commonality in license requirements and job expectations, job duties, in order for there to be kind of cohesive, meaningful bargaining.

The other, I think, really important definition to understand is what is collective bargaining and the balance that we are trying to strike between ushering in this new legal regime, but then also recognizing that the school board maintains ultimate authority to supervise and manage and administer the school division.

That's constitutional, right? And so we're very aware of that. And also, you know, the state collective bargaining statute made very clear that in no way could collective bargaining impair your budgeting authority.

And so the definition of collective bargaining, it is permitted to touch upon any matter relating to employees or their employment or service. That's the language from the collective bargaining statute.

And so we feel that we have defined the term in a way that does that, but then also ensures that the school board's authority is in no way diminished. Next slide. please. And so I think that's a good segue then into this next section, which, you know, the resolution spells out very clearly what rights does the school board maintain that are unfettered and untouched by collective bargaining. And there are certain managerial prerogatives like writing job descriptions, setting your staffing levels, hiring and discharging and promoting and

laying off if there needs to be a reduction in force. And so there's no collective bargaining about those inherent managerial issues, but then also the thing to understand about collective bargaining is at its core, it's about employee free choice, right? There is no collective bargaining if it's not something that employees vote for, and so the resolution has to put employees at its center, so employees have to be able to discuss with one another whether this is of interest to

them or not, and if so, to go about electing their bargaining representative. And so the resolution sets forth a section on employee rights that would be new in Loudoun County public schools, and then also a section on the rights of an exclusive representative if one is elected.

In order for that representative to adequately serve all bargaining unit employees, they have be able to talk to those people, to have access to them, to have their information, be able to send them emails, and be able to represent them in grievances and things like that. And what's critical too is that the representative that employees elect, it's important that the school division honor that selection, right? So it can't negotiate with another organization. That is the one bargaining representative that the you know that the school board through its designees is

permitted to engage in negotiations with about matters that are within the definition of collective bargaining next slide please thank you and then I want to also just touch upon the election process because I think that's very new as well and here again the theme of you know, employee free choice is what's really kind of at the core. Unlike, you know, school board elections that come about on a regular cycle, that's not how union elections work. They have

to be triggered by employees saying that that's what they're interested in. And so the resolution sets forth a process for how employees go about indicating that that's of interest to them and And how many employees would have to show their support for having an election in order to trigger that process.

And here, too, the National Labor Relations Act has been a model. There under federal labor policy, it's 30% of employees in a bargaining unit to trigger an election. And so that's what we've proposed.

elections are traditional democratic elections decided by majority of those who decide to participate and vote. And so that, again, is what we're proposing here. It's really important to keep in mind that all along this process, employees should have the right to completely abstain, right? If they're just not interested in participating in an election, if they're just not interested in signing a union authorization card, if they're just not interested in becoming an LEA member, they have the right to do that. So we're very wary of requiring participation

in the election or requiring a certain percentage of participation should be up to employees to make that choice. And the election will always be by secret ballot. There's a separate state statute that requires that. So, you know, vote, how voters vote is always kept confidential. Intervention is a process by which other interested organizations request to be included on the ballot in an election for an exclusive representative. The requirement for them to get on the ballot is the same as what it would take for LEA to call for an election in the

first place, at least 30% support among employees. And the thing to understand is it's not a zero-sum game. A competing organization can get membership and authorization cards from the same cohort of employees that LEA is working to organize. Once employees vote, they can select only one choice, but they can join as many organizations, sign as many authorization cards for as many different unions as they would like. And then decertification is the process by which employees decide to remove

an exclusive representative after one has been elected. And here, too, we've been really guided by federal labor law. It's important after an election that a representative have a chance to get its bearings, negotiate a first contract. So for that reason, decertification under our proposed resolution isn't permitted within the first year of an election for certification, and then during the term of a contract.

It's important that that contract, it's a legal document and to give that its full force in effect for a party to that agreement to not be decertified mid-contract term. However, there has to be some opportunity for employees to decide if the majority no longer want exclusive representation, there has to be opportunity for them to call for an election.

So the resolution we've proposed sets forth a 30-day window as a three-year contract is about to expire when employees could call for another election. Okay, thank you. Next slide. And then I just wanted to also, I think this is the last bit that I'm going to cover, and then I'm going to turn it over to Corey, bargaining procedures.

So, you know, after a representative is certified as employees-exclusive bargaining representative, you get to really the meat of collective bargaining, and that's sitting down across the table from one another and discussing terms and conditions of employment.

And so, again, in recognition of the fact that the statutory language is somewhat broad, it allows bargaining over any matter relating to employees or their employment or service. And what we propose bargaining over are wages and hours in scheduling, retirement, benefits, health and safety, work rules and evaluations, discipline, quality of life issues, other terms and conditions of employment.

But know that all of this is permissive and none of it is required or mandatory. You know, the sole requirement would be that we come together in good faith. But there's no such thing as mandatory bargaining law in Virginia.

It's all permissive. Whether a resolution is even passed is within the school board's discretion. And there's no overarching state agency or federal agency with jurisdiction over collective bargaining in Virginia that can require negotiations.

So that's always something to keep in mind as well. Impasse, Sandy mentioned this briefly, that's when the two sides can't come to agreement, they've negotiated in good faith and they're just at loggerheads. We propose a process that begins with mediation.

So something that doesn't cost anything, the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service is they're a federal agency. We pay for them already through our tax dollars. They offer experienced mediators who work in the labor relations space are very highly qualified and it's a service that's free of charge.

So we start with something like that and then from there a panel decision that would be final and binding on both sides But the panel would be comprised of a school board appointee, an LEA appointee, and then a neutral upon whom we both agree.

So there, too, we think there are ways to go about resolving conflict that can be cost effective and that allow both the school board and an exclusive representative to continue to have a voice in the process.

And the last thing I'll touch upon is sort of a nuance of the resolution called an evergreen clause, which is a significant part of the collective bargaining landscape. And it states essentially that as we negotiate an agreement, if there's an existing agreement in place, that agreement remains in effect until we have signed off on a new document.

So if negotiations are taking some time and an existing agreement has expired before we've come to agreement on a new one, it's important that the contract terms that we agreed to remain in effect so that we can continue to negotiate improvements.

You can continue to seek things that you would like to change. We can continue to seek things that we may like to change without wiping out progress that was already made. And now I'll turn it over to Corey to cover sort of how we envision actually sitting down and negotiating working.

Because the collective bargaining resolution set forth employee, union, and employer rights, they must also contain a mechanism for enforcing those rights.

Our proposed resolution calls for a cost-effective, multi-step process for resolving allegations. First is an informal meeting with the superintendent. The idea here is if disputes can be resolved informally, we want to encourage that. Step two is a hearing before the school board.

We want the school board involved in this process. The resolution will be a board policy, and it's important for the board to maintain oversight. You do that work already through the existing grievance process.

We are not seeking for collective bargaining to change any of that. Step three would be a panel hearing. Again, on an as-needed basis only, a neutral party skilled in labor relations could be brought in to render a final decision. We feel both would be effective, cost-conscious options. Next slide, please. As we work collectively on the contents of a collective bargaining resolution, we just wanted to again put the process in perspective. A resolution is a necessary first step.

It's a framework. An election must follow passage of a resolution, and LEA must win that election. Then bargaining would begin. Next slide. We wanted to conclude by addressing questions we hear about school divisions' capacity for collective bargaining.

One, a worry about how new this is and about how little is known about it. Will LCPS need a labor relations director and a labor lawyer? The union is not a third party that's going to use a team of lawyers to negotiate a contract. The union is school employees.

School employees are the ones who will be sitting at the table negotiating for improvements to their wages, benefits, and working conditions. We want you to sit down at the table with us, not someone you hired to negotiate on your behalf. We, educators and you, know our school division the best.

We should be the ones negotiating. We'll both have legal counsel to keep us on track, but it's really about us sitting down with you to jointly find solutions to the issues that school employees are facing. You are absolutely within your rights to hire a labor administrator or director in order to facilitate contract negotiations, but you definitely don't need to do so.

Collective bargaining agreements won't be complex legal documents that are difficult to understand. We want employees and their supervisors to be able to read, digest, and implement them. We plan to educate bargaining unit members on their rights under the collective bargaining agreement and envision resolution of issues at the building level.

In Richmond City, the existing HR director negotiated on behalf of the school division. In Prince William, they have brought in labor council on an as-needed basis to partner with their school board council. In Arlington, they did hire a labor relations director, but that is one new position dedicated to implementing the collective bargaining resolution and negotiating collective bargaining agreements.

In Falls Church, the school board initially considered incorporating a new labor relations director position into its resolution and later decided against it. realizing upon the advice of labor council that it was simply unnecessary. They passed a resolution that instead calls for the appointment of a labor relations neutral on an as-needed basis.

Are there topics that we are required to bargain? No. There are no mandatory subjects of bargaining in Virginia. The state collective bargaining statute is entirely permissive, and there is no existing body of collective bargaining case law that establishes mandatory bargaining subjects. In Virginia, all subjects of bargaining are permissive, as we mentioned before, meaning they can, but they don't have to be bargained.

Additionally, the collective bargaining statute left intact Virginia's prohibition on public employee strikes. Entering into contract negotiations with LEA does not open LCPS up to the possibility of a work stoppage or strike. Will collective bargaining cost an arm and a leg? No.

In fact, we know that there are claims out there that school divisions will be required to establish an entire Department of Labor and pay hundreds of thousands in arbitration and contract administration costs. This simply isn't true. You do not need a supervisor of financial services just because you implement a collective bargaining.

You pay your staff now, and employee wages are part of your budget calculations already. Why does discussing pay with staff require you to fill a new role? There's also no need for a new payroll coordinator or other specialized HR staff. You are already deducting dues to LEA from our members' paychecks.

That capacity is there. You also already have databases of employee data that you compile and share. providing that on a regular basis to an exclusive representative does not require additional HR capacity. You have school board policies on standards of professionalism, on grievances, on equal employment opportunity, on discipline, on workplace harassment. You are able to implement those policies with the staff that you have. Placing policies like that within a collective bargaining agreement so that they become collective joint agreements rather than stand-alone board policies does not create a need for new staff with new expertise. The same people who oversee

implementation of those policies as they are posted on board docs can oversee implementation of those policies as they exist in a collective bargaining agreement there are some costs in negotiating an initial contract and electing an exclusive bargaining representative but it will not cost millions or even hundreds of thousands of dollars to sit down with your employees and come to a mutual agreement over working conditions and ways to improve the schools thank you for letting us present we really really really really appreciate it and wanted to know if have any questions for us yeah i appreciate the the work that you did putting together a draft

to those two employee types. So we have worked in collaboration

with other school divisions that have passed these policies in crafting those details. and adding them to the policy that the school board ends up considering and voting on. So we had a joint committee in Falls Church, for example. I worked very closely also with the superintendent and two school board members in Charlottesville.

In Richmond, my boss, our general counsel, worked really closely with their school attorney on resolution language. And it's exactly those kinds of things that we're very much open to considering language that is most suitable for LCPS.

And we'd be happy to have that conversation about ways that, you know, our proposal can be expanded upon, can be tweaked, can be edited to really meet the way that you all envision collective bargaining working here.

Thank you.
